Inspired by Sol LeWitt's instructional wall drawings, he translates written scores into generative software where the artist's role is to define relational rules rather than compose pictures. His Process series (2005-ongoing) explores instruction-based visuals where possibilities for interaction between elements are outlined in code, and structures evolve through element actions within given parameters. Later work (Ultraconcentrated, In Silico, Compressed Cinema) extends into machine learning, using GANs to compress and transform existing media. He also curates and builds infrastructure for digital art through Feral File."}, "relevance_to_sense_room": {"relevance_summary": "Reas's practice is a foundational reference for relational composition in generative art — his Software Structures project explicitly demonstrated how art can emerge from defined relational rules rather than fixed compositions. The Process series generates organic, cell-like visual fields that could serve as ground layers in a composed exhibition environment.", "relational_composition": "Yes, centrally. Rather than pursuing photorealism, they train models to generate uncanny hybrid organisms that exist between categories — part jellyfish, part flower, part something entirely new. The training data curation is an artistic act: selecting which organisms and ecosystems to train on shapes the aesthetic and conceptual territory of the output. Recent work under the Entangled Others banner has expanded to include real-time generative ecosystems, AR installations, and interactive works that respond to environmental data (coral bleaching data, biodiversity metrics). They combine outputs from multiple model architectures and post-process results to create coherent visual worlds."}, "relevance_to_sense_room": {"relevance_summary": "Crespo/Entangled Others demonstrate how neural networks can generate living ecosystemic compositions — visual worlds where organisms relate to each other and their environment. The Entangled Others studio is itself a protocol for collaborative more-than-human creative practice.", "system_designed": "Custom neural network training pipelines for biological imagery generation. metadata: {"original_type": "artist", "status": "confirmed", "source_file": "Suzanne_Treister.json", "full_profile": {"basic_info": {"name": "Suzanne Treister", "type": "artist", "active_years": "1980s-present (pioneer in digital/new media art since early 1990s; painting practice from 1980s)", "location": "London, UK and French Pyrenees (born London, 1958)", "url": "https://www.suzannetreister.net/", "birth_year": 1958, "nationality": "United Kingdom"}, "practice_description": {"medium": "Drawing, watercolour, diagrammatic mapping, tarot decks, video, installation, photography, web-based work", "practice_summary": "Suzanne Treister creates extensive multi-part projects that map hidden connections between technology, power, knowledge, and belief systems through hand-drawn diagrams, alchemical illustrations, and tarot decks. Her work reveals structures that bind power, identity, and knowledge by tracing how information flows through officially unconnected networks across decades of history.", "methodology": "Treister conducts years-long research investigations spanning cybernetics, military history, counterculture, surveillance, science fiction, occult traditions, and emerging technologies. She synthesizes this research into elaborate taxonomies rendered in traditional media — drawing, watercolour, and diagrammatic illustration — deliberately using 'older technologies that I have autonomy over' rather than the digital systems she critiques. Her projects typically comprise hundreds of individual works organized through frameworks like the tarot (78 cards providing a combinatorial system for connecting disparate knowledge domains). The tarot structure functions as an 'encyclopedic format' and 'alchemical hypertext' that enables non-linear navigation of complex historical and technological relationships. She works across the boundary between scientific inquiry and mystical revelation, using speculative and occult knowledge forms to make visible connections that rational taxonomies obscure."}, "relevance_to_sense_room": {"relevance_summary": "Treister's decades-long practice of mapping knowledge networks as art — using diagrams, tarot structures, and relational illustrations — is a foundational precedent for A(DAI)'s graph-curated exhibition concept. HEXEN 2.0 and HEXEN 5.0 demonstrate that a network of ideas, figures, and events can function as a major artwork where the relational structure is the primary content.", "art_as_substrate": "Yes. Treister's diagrams and tarot systems function as substrates that viewers/participants navigate and activate. The HEXEN tarot decks are explicitly designed as tools — they can be used for collective readings that generate new configurations and interpretations of the mapped knowledge. The substrate is the knowledge network itself.", "relational_composition": "Yes, fundamentally. The HEXEN projects are structured as webs of connections between figures, theories, events, and institutions. The five wall-scale diagrams in HEXEN 2.0 explicitly chart relational networks — 'web-like illustrations depicting key figures of the counter cultures which developed in concurrence with governmental technological developments.' The tarot format adds a combinatorial relational layer: each card's meaning shifts depending on its relationships to other cards in a reading.", "self_recomposing": "Partially. The fixed artworks (diagrams, drawings) are static. However, the tarot decks are designed to be used as tools for collective readings — each reading produces a unique relational configuration. Treister explicitly describes the tarot readings as 'a deconstructionist game for analysing and assessing recent history, the present and imagining a future, done so as a collective.' This participatory use introduces a form of recomposition through human interaction, though it is not computational."}, "key_works": {"works": [{"title": "HEXEN 2.0", "year": "2009-2011", "description": "167-part project comprising 5 large wall-scale diagrams, a 78-card tarot deck, photo-text works, video, and website. Maps the interconnected histories of cybernetics, the internet, military research, counterculture, surveillance, and the control society from WWII to the present. Each tarot card depicts a key figure, theory, or event. The diagrams trace how knowledge 'trips' through unofficially connected networks. Acquired by Tate. Exhibited at Science Museum London and internationally.", "relevance": "The most complete precedent for knowledge-network-as-artwork in the HEXEN tradition. Demonstrates that a hand-crafted graph of ideas and actors can function as a major museum-quality artwork. The tarot format shows how a fixed knowledge graph can generate infinite relational readings through combinatorial use — a non-computational analog to A(DAI)'s generative graph curation."}, {"title": "HEXEN 5.0", "year": "2023-2025", "description": "78 tarot works, 6 large diagrams, and AI-prompted works reimagining alchemical visual language (13th-18th century). Addresses the climate emergency, AI, quantum science, and potential solutions for planetary self-regulation. Builds on HEXEN 2.0's methodology while engaging directly with contemporary AI and ecological crises. Published as a tarot deck by Cosmogenesis.", "relevance": "Demonstrates the ongoing vitality and adaptability of knowledge-network mapping as artistic practice. The direct engagement with AI and climate — two central concerns for A(DAI) — makes this the most thematically current precedent. The evolution from HEXEN 2.0 to 5.0 shows how a knowledge graph can be extended and updated over decades."}, {"title": "Prophetic Dreaming (retrospective)", "year": "2025-2027", "description": "First major institutional retrospective spanning 40+ years at Modern Art Oxford (October 2025-April 2026), travelling to Muzeum Sztuki Lodz (2026) and MIMA Middlesbrough (2027). Maps Treister's complete practice of investigating technologies, networks of power, alternative belief systems, and futures they prefigure.", "relevance": "The retrospective format itself demonstrates how a lifelong practice of knowledge mapping accumulates into a meta-graph — Treister's complete body of work IS a decades-spanning relational map of technology, power, and alternative futures."}]}, "protocol_art_resonance": {"protocol_art_summary": "Treister does not design protocols or systems in a technical sense, but her tarot decks function as protocols for collective knowledge navigation. The HEXEN tarot system provides a structured method (draw cards, read relationships, generate interpretation) for groups to collectively analyze historical forces and imagine futures. This is protocol design in a social/participatory sense — creating rules and structures for collective sensemaking.", "system_designed": "The HEXEN tarot system — a combinatorial framework for collective readings that function as group sensemaking sessions. The framework includes 78 cards representing key nodes in a knowledge network, structured according to tarot's major/minor arcana system, designed to be used in group settings for analyzing the present and imagining futures. This is a social protocol for collective intelligence, not a technical one."}, "commons_orientation": {"licence_model": "hybrid", "commons_summary": "Treister's work circulates through the commercial gallery system (represented by Annely Juda Fine Art, P.P.O.W. Gallery) and institutional collections (Tate, Centre Pompidou, Science Museum). However, significant parts of the work are freely accessible through her comprehensive website (suzannetreister.net) and the HEXEN project websites. The tarot decks are published as affordable objects (not limited editions). The knowledge-sharing ethos of the practice — making hidden connections visible — is commons-oriented in spirit, even when the physical artworks circulate commercially. [uncertain]"}, "governance_model": {"governance_type": "solo", "governance_detail": "Solo artistic practice spanning over 40 years. Treister is the sole author, researcher, and creator of all works. The tarot readings introduce a participatory governance element — when used collectively, the group's interpretive choices determine meaning — but the artworks themselves are authored by Treister alone."}, "consent_and_authorship": {"consent_approach": "Not a primary concern for the practice. Treister works with historical and published material — mapping publicly known figures, events, institutions, and theories. No personal data or participant data is used. The tarot readings involve voluntary participation in collective interpretation.", "authorship_model": "Solo authorship. Treister is the sole creator of all works, conducting all research and producing all drawings, diagrams, and illustrations herself. She deliberately chooses hand-drawing and watercolour as media she has full autonomy over, maintaining complete authorial control. No machine co-authorship (she explicitly eschews using AI to make work about AI)."}, "liveness_and_duration": {"temporal_type": "static", "temporal_detail": "Individual artworks are fixed — hand-drawn diagrams, watercolours, and prints that do not change. However, the tarot decks introduce a performative temporal dimension: each group reading produces a unique configuration in real-time. The practice itself has a durational quality — HEXEN evolved from 2.0 (2009-2011) to 5.0 (2023-2025), showing how a knowledge mapping project extends and recomposes across decades. The websites remain accessible as living reference documents."}, "data_materiality": {"data_sources": "Historical research spanning cybernetics, military history, intelligence agencies, counterculture movements, science fiction, occult traditions, quantum science, AI research, climate science, philosophy, sociology, and political theory. Sources include published histories, declassified documents, academic research, biographical information about key figures, and speculative/fictional texts.", "data_provenance": "Entirely from published, public-domain, and historical sources. No scraped data, no personal data, no institutional datasets. The research is traditional scholarly/investigative work synthesized through artistic practice. Fully transparent provenance — all figures and events depicted are identifiable and verifiable."}, "embedding_space_relevance": {"embedding_summary": "Treister does not work with computational embedding spaces. However, her practice is conceptually analogous: she manually 'embeds' historical figures, events, theories, and institutions in a relational space (the diagram) based on their connections and influences. The tarot structure provides a fixed dimensional framework (78 positions) within which knowledge is embedded. This is a human-authored, non-computational form of relational embedding.", "multimodal": "Works span visual (drawings, watercolours, diagrams), textual (research, card descriptions), video, and web modalities, but these are not computationally unified. They are complementary presentations of the same research program."}, "exhibition_modality": {"modality": "hybrid", "spatial_description": "Works manifest as: (1) large wall-scale diagrams that viewers navigate physically, tracing connections across the surface, (2) framed watercolours and drawings arranged in grids or sequences, (3) tarot decks as portable, handleable objects used in collective readings, (4) video animations, (5) websites for digital navigation. The physical exhibition experience involves moving between wall diagrams and individual drawings, piecing together the relational network across the gallery space. The tarot deck can be used outside the gallery in participatory settings."}, "sensory_register": {"senses": "visual, textual", "dominant_register": "visual"}, "interoperability": {"composability": "The tarot deck format is inherently composable — cards can be combined in infinite configurations for readings. The knowledge network depicted in the diagrams could theoretically be digitized into a graph database, though Treister has not done this. The content is highly composable at a conceptual level (figures, events, and connections could be integrated into larger knowledge systems) but is not technically interoperable in its current form.", "technical_openness": "The artworks are physically open (exhibited, published, accessible on her website) but not technically open in the sense of APIs, standard formats, or machine-readable data. The knowledge is embedded in hand-drawn visual form rather than structured data."}, "technical_approach": {"stack": "Traditional art media: drawing, watercolour, pen and ink. Video production tools. Web development for project websites. Photography. Treister deliberately avoids using the technologies she critiques — she uses 'older technologies like drawing and watercolour that I have autonomy over and are not dependent on the technologies I might be examining.' No ML, no generative software, no blockchain, no code-based art. The 'technology' is research methodology and the tarot's combinatorial structure."}, "network_position": {"position_type": "bridge", "scene_affiliation": "Contemporary art (Tate, Centre Pompidou, Modern Art Oxford), new media art (pioneer since 1990s), critical technology art, digital culture critique, speculative/science fiction art, occult/esoteric art traditions. Bridges the contemporary art mainstream with critical technology discourse, and bridges rational/scientific analysis with esoteric/occult knowledge frameworks. Connected to London's art and technology scene, European new media art networks.", "connections": "Vladan Joler (shared practice of diagrammatic knowledge mapping as art — Joler maps technological infrastructure, Treister maps historical/political/occult knowledge networks; both use the relational diagram as primary artistic form and both are in major institutional collections). Both represent the 'graph-as-art' tradition that is the most direct precedent for A(DAI)."}, "potential_role_in_adai": {"role": "theoretical-reference", "role_detail": "Treister's practice provides A(DAI) with: (1) a 40-year precedent for knowledge-network mapping as a legitimate and major art form, (2) the tarot as a model for combinatorial knowledge navigation — a non-computational protocol for collective sensemaking through relational reading, (3) a critique of techno-solutionism from within the art-technology space (her refusal to use AI to discuss AI is a principled position A(DAI) should consider), (4) evidence that hand-crafted, human-authored knowledge graphs have enduring value (Tate acquisition, ongoing retrospective). HEXEN's evolution from 2.0 to 5.0 across 15 years shows how a knowledge mapping project can grow and adapt. Her tarot-based collective reading protocol could inspire A(DAI)'s approach to participatory knowledge navigation."}, "temporal_status": {"status": "ongoing-practice"}, "uncertain": ["commons_summary"]}, "data_provenance": {"source": "seed-research-2025", "confidence": "high", "trust_tier": "reviewed"}, "wikidata_qid": "Q19508923"}

metadata: {"original_type": "artist", "status": "confirmed", "source_file": "Tabita_Rezaire.json", "full_profile": {"basic_info": {"name": "Tabita Rezaire", "type": "artist", "active_years": "2012-present", "location": "Cayenne, French Guiana (formerly Paris, Johannesburg)", "url": "https://www.tabitarezaire.com", "birth_year": 1989, "nationality": "France"}, "practice_description": {"medium": "Video, installation, immersive environments, digital art, performance, healing practices, VR", "practice_summary": "French Guianese artist working across new media, healing practices, and ancestral knowledge systems to challenge the colonial and extractive frameworks embedded in digital technology. Her work connects internet infrastructure, data colonialism, and algorithmic bias to longer histories of extraction, proposing indigenous and spiritual knowledge as alternative technological paradigms.", "methodology": "Rezaire combines deep research into technology infrastructure (undersea cables, satellite systems, internet governance) with study of African, South American, and indigenous healing and knowledge traditions (Kemetic yoga, plant medicine, ancestral technologies). She produces high-saturation digital video works that layer internet aesthetics (memes, screen recordings, browser windows) over spiritual and decolonial content. Increasingly, her practice has moved toward embodied healing work -- kundalini yoga, doula practice, and land-based projects at her space in French Guiana (Amakaba). She holds an MFA from Goldsmiths and studied at Wits School of Arts, Johannesburg."}, "relevance_to_sense_room": {"relevance_summary": "Rezaire's practice directly challenges the extractive knowledge frameworks that A(DAI) seeks to avoid. Rezaire's work is fundamentally relational -- it maps connections between undersea cables and colonial trade routes, between internet governance and resource extraction, between ancestral knowledge and digital technology. Amakaba in French Guiana functions as a proto-protocol for land-based, decolonial knowledge production.", "system_designed": "Amakaba: a residency and healing space in French Guiana that functions as alternative infrastructure for knowledge production outside Western institutional frameworks. She advocates for knowledge commons rooted in indigenous and ancestral traditions rather than Western open-source models."}, "governance_model": {"governance_type": "solo", "governance_detail": "Solo artistic practice with community-oriented projects. Her healing practice operates through facilitator-participant structures."}, "consent_and_authorship": {"consent_approach": "Rezaire's decolonial framework implies deep attention to consent, particularly regarding the extraction and representation of indigenous and ancestral knowledge. Her healing practice requires participant consent. metadata: {"original_type": "artist", "status": "confirmed", "source_file": "Tega_Brain.json", "full_profile": {"basic_info": {"name": "Tega Brain", "type": "artist", "active_years": "2013-present", "location": "New York, USA (originally Sydney, Australia)", "url": "https://tegabrain.com", "nationality": "Australia"}, "practice_description": {"medium": "Installation, software, environmental systems, data infrastructure, writing, web-based work", "practice_summary": "Artist and engineer whose practice interrogates environmental data systems, infrastructure governance, and the politics of optimization. She builds alternative environmental management systems that expose how data collection, algorithmic decision-making, and infrastructure design encode specific political and ecological values.", "methodology": "Brain creates functioning technological systems that propose alternative logics for environmental management -- using AI to make deliberately eccentric land-use decisions, building real eccentric water treatment systems, and creating tools that reveal hidden data infrastructure. She combines environmental engineering (background in environmental engineering and interaction design) with art practice, teaching at NYU's ITP program. Her methodology involves building working systems that follow non-optimized logics, revealing by contrast the assumptions embedded in conventional infrastructure. She collaborates with scientists, engineers, and other artists, and has co-authored educational materials on machine learning (co-authored 'AI Art' book with Sam Lavigne)."}, "relevance_to_sense_room": {"relevance_summary": "Brain's practice demonstrates how data infrastructure and environmental systems function as artistic medium. Her work makes visible the governance decisions embedded in data collection and algorithmic management -- directly relevant to how a graph-curated exhibition encodes curatorial values in its infrastructure.", "art_as_substrate": "Partial -- her environmental systems (Asunder, Eccentric Engineering) create infrastructural substrates that produce environmental outcomes. The data pipelines and AI decision systems function as ground layers, but outputs are environmental conditions and policy proposals rather than artworks that others compose with.", "relational_composition": "Yes -- Asunder composes relationships between environmental datasets (satellite imagery, weather data, soil data, water systems) to generate land management proposals. metadata: {"original_type": "artist", "status": "bridge", "source_file": "Harold_Cohen.json", "full_profile": {"basic_info": {"name": "Harold Cohen", "type": "artist", "active_years": "1960s-2016", "location": "United Kingdom / United States (born London 1928; d. Encinitas CA 2016)", "url": null, "birth_year": 1928, "nationality": "United Kingdom"}, "practice_description": {"practice_summary": "British-American painter who, from 1973, developed AARON — a computer programme that autonomously made drawings and, later, colour paintings. Cohen spent four decades evolving AARON through hand-authored rule-based code, expanding its repertoire from abstract line drawings through figurative compositions (people in jungles, gardens) to colour image-making. AARON is the single longest-running artist-authored AI project in art history: one artist, one machine collaborator that grew and changed, forty-three years. Cohen treated AARON not as a tool and not as an autonomous agent in the contemporary sense, but as a colleague whose rule-set he continually revised. His writings — especially 'The Further Exploits of AARON, Painter' — frame this work as a sustained investigation into what machine-making can illuminate about human-making. He resisted framings that treated AARON as either mere tool or as approaching genuine creativity; his position was subtler and worked out in code.", "methodology": "Slow, sustained, hand-authored symbolic AI. Cohen wrote AARON in C (earlier versions in LISP-adjacent environments), progressively encoding knowledge: how to draw a figure, how to compose a scene, how to select colour, how to balance a composition. Each expansion was an artistic decision implemented as a code change. No machine learning; no neural networks; no training data beyond Cohen's own continual rule-authoring. The paintings themselves were executed by a robotic painting machine Cohen designed, spraying or brushing pigment onto canvas as directed by AARON's compositional output.", "medium": "code (C, earlier LISP-adjacent), autonomous drawing and painting programmes, robotic painting hardware, oil on canvas, acrylic, print, critical writing"}, "key_works": {"works": [{"title": "AARON", "year": "1973-2016 (continuous)", "description": "The programme itself, in its successive versions across four decades. Treated as a single evolving artwork — not a series of discrete pieces — though it produced thousands of drawings and hundreds of paintings along the way. Each version represents Cohen's current position on what AARON can and should be able to do.", "relevance": "Foundational for every subsequent conversation about AI art. The canonical prior art for any 2020s generative-AI-in-art claim. Unique in being simultaneously software, artwork, collaborator, and decades-long sustained artistic project."}, {"title": "AARON-generated drawings (1970s-80s jungle series)", "year": "1977-1985", "description": "Early colour drawings produced by AARON during its 'people in jungles' figurative period. Displayed at Computer Museum Boston, Tate, and the Stedelijk. The aesthetic — child-like, vivid, confident line — was a deliberate product of the knowledge Cohen had encoded at that stage.", "relevance": "The visual register most strongly associated with AARON in public memory. Widely reproduced in AI-art histories."}, {"title": "AARON colour paintings (late 1990s-2000s)", "year": "1995-2010", "description": "Large-format oil and acrylic canvases produced via Cohen's custom robotic painting machines, directed by AARON. Still-life, botanical, and figurative compositions with a distinctive tonal logic that arose from the colour rules Cohen spent years refining.", "relevance": "Extends AARON into painting proper, not only drawing; demonstrates that the project could adapt across media while retaining authorial coherence."}]}, "network_position": {"scene_affiliation": "early AI art pioneers (pre-deep-learning era); UC San Diego Centre for Research in Computing and the Arts (CRCA); symbolic-AI research community", "connections": "Edward Feigenbaum (AI researcher, Stanford; long collaborator-interlocutor), Margaret Boden (philosopher of creativity; wrote extensively on AARON), Lillian Schwartz (parallel 1970s computer-art generation), Mario Klingemann (heir in GAN-era AI art), Anna Ridler (heir in dataset-era AI art), Sofia Crespo (heir)"}, "commons_orientation": {"commons_summary": "Cohen's writings and AARON's principles are publicly available; code has been partially released (Whitney has a working installation; Tate holds related materials). But the specific working AARON code as Cohen used it at any given moment was a personal studio artefact, not an open-source project. The Gazelli Art House and the Cohen estate have since curated partial releases."}, "governance_model": "Single-author studio practice with institutional partners (UCSD CRCA) for computing resources. Posthumous governance now distributed between the Cohen estate, Gazelli Art House (representing the work commercially and curatorially), Tate, and the Whitney.", "consent_and_authorship": "Cohen was insistent and public about authorship: he was the artist; AARON was his collaborator and medium. This resists the current convention of framing AI outputs as 'made by the AI' — a framing Cohen explicitly rejected as both technically inaccurate and historically lazy. A(DAI) treats this authorship position as a primary resource.", "liveness_and_duration": "Both. The programme is live (can run and produce new output); the paintings and drawings are fixed. Running AARON today requires maintaining an old computing environment or porting the code; both partial preservations exist.", "data_materiality": {"data_sources": "None in the modern ML sense — AARON was not trained. Its 'knowledge' is the rule-set Cohen wrote. He theorised this as 'arte concreta semântica' (semantic concrete art): the computer's capacity to operate on meaning, not only on form. name: Academic Media-Art History
metadata: {"status": "draft", "source_file": "Lens_Academic_Media_Art_History.json", "full_profile": {"basic_info": {"name": "Academic Media-Art History", "type": "classification_lens", "slug": "academic-media-art-history", "active_years": "1960s-present", "location": "distributed (major hubs: Karlsruhe, Linz, Cambridge MA, Montreal, Melbourne, Donau-Universität Krems)", "url": null}, "description": "The canonising logic of scholarly media-art history — the field consolidated by Oliver Grau's research networks, the Leonardo/MIT Press journal and book series since 1968, the MediaArtHistories conference circuit, ACM SIGGRAPH's historical record, and university programmes in digital humanities and media archaeology. This lens frames digital art through genealogy: who came before whom, what earlier technologies or ideas this work recovers or extends, how a specific practice fits a longer arc that includes pre-computer cybernetic art, concrete poetry, conceptual art, and scientific visualisation. It values provenance of ideas, cites other works carefully, and is structurally weak at immediately legible market or viral art — it waits. It is the slowest of the five lenses; its canonical judgements take decades to form, but they outlast the others. Pioneer-era practitioners (Cohen, Nake, Molnar, Schwartz, Mohr, Csuri, Komura) owe much of their current visibility to this lens rather than to market or immediate-institutional readings.", "exemplars": ["Harold Cohen / AARON (bridge practitioner — academic coverage predates institutional market recognition)", "Lillian Schwartz (bridge — Bell Labs + academic writing)", "Waldemar Cordeiro (bridge — ICAA / Latin American academic archive)", "Masao Komura / CTG (bridge — SIGGRAPH Pioneers + MediaArtHistories retrospectives)", "Prema Murthy (bridge — Rhizome + academic feminist media writing)", "Hito Steyerl (heavy academic citation; e-flux journal; Duty Free Art)", "Matteo Pasquinelli (theorist — academic media-critical scholarship)", "McKenzie Wark (theorist — critical media theory)", "Legacy Russell (theorist — Glitch Feminism)", "Yuk Hui (theorist — philosophy of technology)"], "blind_spots": "Very recent practice (the lens is slow; anything younger than ~5 years tends to be under-covered even when genuinely significant). Practice whose documentation lives only on social platforms or chat servers, which academic publishing cycles can't easily cite. Practitioners who refuse academic engagement.", "classification_logic": "Apply this lens when the practitioner or work has substantial scholarly coverage — peer-reviewed articles, academic monographs, inclusion in conference proceedings (MediaArtHistories, SIGGRAPH historical papers, Leonardo journal), university teaching use — OR when the practitioner is themselves a working theorist whose writing is part of the academic corpus (Pasquinelli, Wark, Russell, Hui, Steyerl). name: Crypto Market-Native
metadata: {"status": "draft", "source_file": "Lens_Crypto_Market_Native.json", "full_profile": {"basic_info": {"name": "Crypto Market-Native", "type": "classification_lens", "slug": "crypto-market-native", "active_years": "2014-present", "location": "on-chain (Ethereum, Tezos, Bitcoin, Base, Solana) + associated platforms", "url": null}, "description": "The canonising logic of on-chain markets and platforms — Foundation, Art Blocks, fxhash, SuperRare, Manifold, Objkt, Zora, Highlight, Verse. This lens reads practice through on-chain provenance: who minted what, on which contract, when, to whom. Editions, secondary sales, auction records, curator-seal platforms, and the history of a wallet address carry weight equivalent to exhibition records. It is native to generative art (Art Blocks, fxhash) and to artist-contract culture (Manifold), and it collapses authorship, edition, and market-price into a single chain of cryptographically-signed events. It excels at tracking participation, community formation around drops, and the economic life of a work. It is structurally incapable of reading pre-2014 practice and has a shallow grasp of critical contexts that lived off-chain. Its canonising speed is extraordinary — Fidenza became a genre reference within months of release — but its retention depends on continued market interest.", "exemplars": ["Art Blocks (platform; the genre-defining on-chain generative art platform)", "fxhash (Tezos generative-art platform)", "Harm van den Dorpel (early adopter; chain-native practice)", "Jonas Lund (system-native conceptual crypto work)", "Sarah Friend (smart-contract-as-medium)", "Fellowship (curatorial on-chain)", "Feral File (curatorial digital editions)", "Metalabel (collective on-chain publishing)", "Tyler Hobbs / Fidenza (canon-forming within this lens)", "Kevin McCoy / Quantum (first NFT; foundational on-chain history)"], "blind_spots": "Pre-2014 practice in its entirety. Practice where the artwork is off-chain but the artist is on-chain-active — the lens tends to read these as 'web2 artists who also mint' rather than recognise the primary body of work. name: Euro-American Institutional
metadata: {"status": "draft", "source_file": "Lens_Euro_American_Institutional.json", "full_profile": {"basic_info": {"name": "Euro-American Institutional", "type": "classification_lens", "slug": "euro-american-institutional", "active_years": "1960s-present", "location": "distributed (major centres: New York, London, Basel, Karlsruhe, Berlin)", "url": null}, "description": "The canonising logic of major Euro-American museums, kunsthalles, and flagship commissioning institutions — MoMA, Tate, the Whitney, Centre Pompidou, Serpentine, ZKM, HEK, Haus der Kulturen der Welt, major biennales. This lens reads digital art through the categories institutions have spent a century refining: the named practitioner as author, the discrete work as object (or timed performance), the exhibition as site, acquisition as validation, and the critical essay as afterlife. It tends to foreground works that translate into institutional formats — prints, editions, installations that travel, commissions that fit programme cycles. It is deeply literate in art-historical lineage and weak at reading work that lives natively on platforms or in network protocols. Institutions are slowly adapting: MoMA's acquisition of Anadol (2023), the Herndon/Dryhurst Holly+ commission (Serpentine), and Beeple's Christie's moment forced the lens to widen. But the logic beneath — the named maker, the primary object, the discrete exhibition — persists.", "exemplars": ["Casey Reas (Processing; widely institutional since 2001)", "Refik Anadol (MoMA acquisition 2023)", "Hito Steyerl (documenta, Venice, Tate)", "Holly Herndon (Serpentine Holly+ commission)", "Mario Klingemann (Sotheby's, MoMA)", "Anna Ridler (Barbican, V&A, ZKM)", "Sougwen Chung (Asian Art Museum, Cooper Hewitt)", "Ian Cheng (MoMA PS1, Serpentine Emissaries)", "teamLab (through its global museum tours)"], "blind_spots": "Practice that lives in platforms, DAOs, chat servers, or code repositories and never produces a discrete exhibitable object. name: Practitioner Self-Report
metadata: {"status": "draft", "source_file": "Lens_Practitioner_Self_Report.json", "full_profile": {"basic_info": {"name": "Practitioner Self-Report", "type": "classification_lens", "slug": "practitioner-self-report", "active_years": "ongoing", "location": "wherever the practitioner is", "url": null}, "description": "The practitioner's own account of their work, lineage, and position. Per CLAUDE.md §Trust Model, self-report from an artist about their own practice carries the highest epistemic authority in A(DAI) — higher than curatorial framing, academic writing, or market activity. The artist knows which tool they actually used, who they were thinking about, what the work contests, and which readings misread it. This lens is the project's editorial commitment to treating the artist as a primary source, not a subject to be canonised about. It is structurally different from the other four lenses: those read the field from the outside-in (the institution, the market, the academy, the regional gatekeeper). This one reads from the inside-out. It is also, crucially, the one this graph has the least of at first-pass: almost all 59 existing practitioner JSONs were researched about artists by outside authors. The self-report lens is therefore scaffolded now, empty for most nodes, and will fill in over time as practitioners join and edit their own claims.", "exemplars": ["Holly Herndon + Mat Dryhurst (Spawning; Holly+ — practitioners building their own infrastructure)", "Grimes / Elf.Tech (artist-authored voice-model platform)", "K Allado-McDowell (AI-collaborative practice theorised by the practitioner themselves)", "Danielle Brathwaite-Shirley (artist-written accompanying texts drive the reading)", "Tabita Rezaire (artist-led cosmology frames the work's meaning)", "[scaffolded — the majority of this lens is intentionally empty at first-pass]"], "blind_spots": "Practitioners who are deceased, inactive, or uninterested in self-documenting. Practice where the artist deliberately refuses self-authorship (anonymous, pseudonymous, or collectively-authored-without-spokesperson work). Language barriers — self-report in non-English is under-represented until translation is part of the ingestion flow. Cases where the artist's self-account conflicts with documented facts — the lens does not auto-resolve conflicts; it holds both.", "classification_logic": "Apply this lens when a significant portion of the practitioner-node's metadata was authored or closely reviewed by the practitioner themselves. In practice, at first-pass this means almost none of the existing 59 — flag the lens as scaffolded-empty and surface it as a gap. Populate progressively as practitioners join Layer 3 (the intimate layer in the seed-doc) and contribute their own claims. A practitioner with BOTH euro-american-institutional AND practitioner-self-report tags is epistemically stronger than one with institutional tagging alone.", "data_provenance": {"source": "curated-2026-04", "authored_by": "ai-draft", "references_consulted": ["CLAUDE.md §Trust model (practitioner self-report = highest authority)", "CLAUDE.md §Principles #1 ('show the bias') and #18 ('the practitioner's sensing capacity is the primary intelligence source')", "seed-doc Layer 3 (the intimate layer)"], "reviewed": false, "reviewed_by": null, "reviewed_date": null, "notes": "Draft for human review. Honest admission: at first-pass this lens is largely empty — the point is to make that emptiness visible as a gap the graph is committed to filling, not to paper over it with misclassifications."}}, "data_provenance": {"source": "seed-research-2025-lens-drafts", "confidence": "high", "trust_tier": "reviewed"}}

name: Myriad (Tulips)
metadata: {"status": "confirmed", "description": "Installation displaying all 10,000 hand-photographed and individually labeled tulip images used to train a GAN.
